title: empirical-backpressure-and-prefill-effects-on-continuous-batching
body:
Purpose:
Quick running notes and outcomes from the empirical experiments investigating how upstream backpressure and request prefill behavior interact with our continuous batcher. Trying to capture concrete observations, a reproducible microbenchmark setup, and actionable mitigations to reduce p99 tail regressions while preserving throughput.

Context / why this matters:
- Several production incidents in Nov/Dec where increased traffic variance + warmup prefill heuristics caused sudden bursts of very large batches that amplified token-level contention and produced 2–3x p99 spikes on served models.
- Hypothesis: our current prefill logic (greedy fill to batch_capacity whenever a fast surge is present) combined with upstream retries/backpressure allows large, cold batches to appear that block small high-priority requests.

High-level goals for the experiment:
- Measure how different prefill caps and backpressure levels affect batch size distribution, p50/p95/p99, and fairness (latency breakdown by priority).
- Test simple mitigations: per-priority prefill caps, adaptive timeout scaling, and admission-based small-batch reservations.
- Produce a short playbook for the scheduler owners with recommended defaults and follow-up experiments.

Test harness / reproducible setup (local cluster + CI-run):
- 4x A100-equivalent GPU nodes (simulated in CI with smaller batch caps but same scheduling codepath).
- Runtime build: scheduler v2.14.3 + tracing hooks (microtrace id, span: enqueue/dequeue/kvcache).
- Workload generator: traffic-mix tool (github://redwood/traffic-mix) with these scenarios:
  * steady-qps: 100 qps, 90% small requests (<=32 tokens), 10% large (>=512 tokens)
  * bursty-jitter: baseline 50 qps with Poisson bursts up to 800 qps for 200ms windows
  * backpressure-probe: upstream returns 503/retry signals on 20% of requests during warmup window
- Priority classes: high (interactive, latency-sensitive), normal (standard), low (batch).
- Metrics collected: batch_size_histogram, batch_wait_time_ms, queue_length, per-priority latency quantiles (p50/p90/p95/p99), tail-blocker counts (num small requests waiting behind large batch > 50ms).
- Duration: 30m per run, repeated 10 runs per config to get stable p99.

Configs tested (matrix):
- prefill_cap: none (current prod behavior), capped_0.5 (max 50% of batch capacity filled by prefill), capped_per_priority (high:10%, normal:30%, low:60%), no_prefill
- timeout_base: 3ms, 8ms, 20ms
- admission_enabled: true/false (small-batch reservation 8 slots per GPU)
- backpressure_rate: 0%, 10%, 20% (simulated upstream 503s)

Key observations (empirical):
1) Uncapped prefill + backpressure -> bimodal batch size distribution and large tail
   - median batch size: 12 tokens (for mixed workload), but a heavy second mode at full batch capacity during burst windows
   - p99 increased by 180–220% relative to no-prefill when backpressure_rate >=10%
   - small high-priority requests often observed waiting > 120ms behind a large prefilled batch because dequeue is FIFO in current implementation

2) Per-priority caps significantly reduce worst-case blocking
   - capped_per_priority reduced p99 for high-priority class by ~55% on average across bursty runs (example: from 410ms -> 185ms)
   - throughput loss negligible (<3% tokens/sec) for our test models because prefill was mostly filling low-priority slots that didn't affect steady throughput

3) Timeout scaling helps but is insufficient alone
   - increasing timeout_base from 3ms -> 20ms reduces batch churn but increases median latency for small requests under steady load (expected tradeoff)
   - combining timeout=8ms with capped_per_priority gives better end-to-end tradeoff than either alone

4) Admission/small-batch reservation is the most robust single mitigation for fairness
   - reserving N slots for small/high-priority requests prevents starvation even under heavy prefill/backpressure
   - measured p99 for high-priority with admission_enabled stayed <220ms across all backpressure_rate settings in our runs
   - cost: ~1.6% drop in overall GPU utilization on bursty runs (tradeoff acceptable for SLAed tenants)

5) Interaction with kv-cache: prefilling big batches that include cached prefixes increases effective CPU decode time per token due to cache warmup spikes; leads to longer batch execution and amplifies head-of-line blocking.

Representative numbers (one run, bursty-jitter, backpressure 20%):
- Config: uncapped_prefill, timeout=3ms
  * batch size p50/p95/p99 = 10 / 48 / 96
  * high-priority p50/p95/p99 latency = 12ms / 180ms / 430ms
  * tokens/sec GPU = 158k
- Config: capped_per_priority, timeout=8ms, admission_enabled=true
  * batch size p50/p95/p99 = 9 / 24 / 36
  * high-priority p50/p95/p99 latency = 10ms / 55ms / 190ms
  * tokens/sec GPU = 155k

Microtrace examples (attached traces in linked artifacts):
- trace-2024-12-15-01: small request enqueued, blocked for 132ms behind a large prefilled batch, shows dequeue start -> kvcache miss -> long decode due to model kernel preheating
- trace-2024-12-15-07: admission_enabled run showing small request dequeues within 5ms even during burst period

Open questions / unresolved notes:
- Are there scenarios where per-priority caps cause oscillation (low-priority backlog grows, causing downstream capacity thrash)? initial sims show mild backlog growth but no oscillation over 30m; need longer runs and production trace replay.
- How does prefill interact with model quantization and per-sequence memory pressure? observed occasional OOM signals when large prefilled batches coincide with long sequences and kv-cache growth. Need memory-pressure-aware prefill cap.
- Does admission reservation require cross-GPU coordination in multi-GPU pools? current implementation reserves slots per-GPU which is simpler but can be suboptimal for skewed traffic distribution.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
- Roll out capped_per_priority as default in canary pool (scheduler config flag: prefill_policy: per_priority_caps) with conservative caps (high:15%, normal:35%, low:50%).
- Enable admission reservation for SLA tiers (configurable slots_per_gpu for tier). Start with 8 small slots for high-priority per GPU.
- Keep timeout_base at 8ms for canary pool; monitor median latency and throughput.
- Add a telemetry counter: "prefill_large_batch_blockers" (count small requests delayed >50ms behind a batch > 2x avg batch size) and alert on >100/min sustained.

Medium-term experiments:
- Implement memory-aware prefill (cap prefill size by estimated kv-cache growth + free GPU memory threshold).
- Explore cooperative dequeue: allow high-priority stealing from in-flight batch if execution not started (requires careful rollback semantics).
- Trace-replay production logs for longer windows (72h) to validate no oscillation under real traffic mixes.

To-do / next steps:
- [ ] PR#5176: add per-priority prefill config + admission reservation hooks (owner: Aisha) -> link in linked_artifacts
- [ ] Run 72h replay on staging cluster (owner: Jorge)
- [ ] Add telemetry and alert (owner: Leah)
- [ ] Prepare canary rollout plan and SLO adjustments (owner: Marcus)

Notes to reviewer:
- This is an exploratory doc; kept results intentionally in raw numbers. If we agree on actions I'll prepare a cleaned playbook for product/ops and a short runbook for SRE.
- Slack thread with initial incident notes: slack://C01234567/thread-89 (see linked artifacts).

Appendix: quick checklist for canary rollout
- bump scheduler config: prefill_policy=capped_per_priority, timeout_base=8ms, admission_slots=8
- enable telemetry prefilling counters and hook alert in pagerduty for >100/min small-blocker events
- run model smoke tests (long sequences + kv-cache heavy) before full shift

End of notes.
